key_insight: An AI safety monitor can appear much more or less reliable depending on how its test attacks are generated and optimized. In a case study of a former production OpenAI monitor, measured false negative rates ranged from 0.5% to 20.8%.
problem_solved: Monitor evaluations use simulated attacks as stand-ins for dangerous deployment behavior, but the choice and optimization of those attacks can distort estimates of monitor reliability.
method: Evaluate a former production OpenAI monitor on transcripts generated by attack policies.
Compare measured false negative rates across attack-generation methods and optimization levels.
Measure how sensitive apparent monitor reliability is to the evaluation's attack-policy choices.
impact: Practitioners should treat monitor scores as dependent on the attacks used to test them, not as fixed measures of safety. Testing across varied attack-generation methods and optimization levels can reveal weaknesses that a single evaluation misses.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: attack policy → agent transcript → monitor → flag or miss.
Range chart highlighting the reported 0.5%–20.8% false negative rates.
Comparison grid showing attack-generation method and optimization level as evaluation variables.
Warning icon with the caption: “Test attack selection shapes apparent safety.”
paper_title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
paper_authors: Charlie Griffin, Oliver Makins, Asa Cooper Stickland, Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal
